questiontext.text: Which best describes the core mechanism of bucket sort?

answer.text: Scatter elements into buckets by value range, sort each bucket, then concatenate the buckets in order

feedback.text: Correct — scatter, sort within each bucket, then gather.

answer.text: Repeatedly swap adjacent out-of-order elements until the array is sorted

feedback.text: That describes bubble sort, not bucket sort.

answer.text: Recursively pick a pivot and partition the array around it

feedback.text: That is quicksort, a comparison sort.

answer.text: Build a binary heap and repeatedly extract the maximum

feedback.text: That is heapsort.

generalfeedback.text: Bucket sort distributes elements across k buckets according to their value range, sorts each bucket (often with insertion sort), and concatenates.

questiontext.text: For inputs uniformly distributed over the range and spread into k buckets, what is the average-case time complexity of bucket sort?

feedback.text: Correct — uniform inputs put ~constant elements per bucket, so scatter and gather dominate.
That is the comparison-sort lower bound; bucket sort beats it under a distribution assumption.
That is the worst case, not the average.
You must at least touch every element once to place it.

generalfeedback.text: With uniform distribution each bucket holds O(1) elements on average, so the total work is O(n + k).

answer.text: A skewed distribution where nearly all elements land in a single bucket, so the per-bucket sort dominates

feedback.text: Correct — one overloaded bucket degrades to the cost of its inner sort.

answer.text: Using more buckets than there are elements

feedback.text: Extra empty buckets do not create quadratic behavior.
Sorted uniform input is still fine; it is skew, not order, that hurts.
Stability of the inner sort does not affect the worst-case bound.

generalfeedback.text: If the distribution is skewed so that one bucket receives O(n) elements, sorting that bucket costs O(n^2) with a comparison inner sort.

questiontext.text: Bucket sort is stable provided the sort used within each bucket is stable and elements are appended in input order.

feedback.text: Correct — stability is inherited from a stable per-bucket sort.
Bucket sort can be stable when the inner sort is stable.

questiontext.text: Bucket sort is a comparison-based sorting algorithm that is bound by the Ω(n log n) lower bound.

feedback.text: No — bucket sort assumes a distribution over the key range, so it is not purely comparison-based.
Correct — it distributes by value and can beat the comparison lower bound.

questiontext.text: Elements are scattered into containers, each covering a sub-range of values, called a ______ (singular English term).

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Bucket sort achieves its O(n + k) average time when the input is assumed to be ______ distributed over the range (fill in the English word, e.g. "uniform").

feedback.text: Correct.
Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about bucket sort are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Its auxiliary space is O(n + k) for the buckets

feedback.text: Yes — space grows with both the elements and the number of buckets.

answer.text: It works well when values are spread evenly across a known range

feedback.text: Yes — a uniform spread keeps buckets small.

answer.text: It performs no work proportional to the number of buckets

feedback.text: No — scattering and concatenation cost depends on k.

answer.text: It guarantees O(n log n) regardless of the input distribution

feedback.text: No — a skewed distribution degrades it to O(n^2).

generalfeedback.text: Bucket sort uses O(n + k) space, thrives on uniform inputs, does k-proportional scatter/gather work, and degrades on skew.
